Copenhagen, December 15, 1848. At the twenty seventh meeting of the Danish National Assembly, held yesteiday, the first moiion on the order of the day, was a question, or, as it is called þÿ þÿ to the Ministry, on the situation of our West India Colonies, put by the much esteemed member for the second electoral district of this city ; H. P. Hansen, Esq. merchant and one of the principal Directors of the National or State Bank of Denmatk. For the information of our fellow citizens and friends in the colonies tfiis report is forwarded, þÿ containing particulars of this interesting meeting fiaketi from the official þÿ þÿliigsdagstidende ; ) it will be observed, that many important matters have been touched upon, and that the Government appears inclined to take due notice of ah just claims, made from the colonies, respecting compensation, organisation of labour, administrative reforms and colonial Representation; it will now rest with the Colonists themselves to embody their rational wishes in the form of loyal petitions and to express their hope and desires to the Government Commissary, now empowered with the supreme administration of II. M. Government in our island. II P. Hansen rose and said : The question, 1 have to make, and of which I have given due notice to the Hon. President, is as billows ; þÿ þÿ Can the d\lmistry explain from the reports it may have received. in how far our West India Colonies and i In i interests and prosperity of the inhabitants may hare been matei tally affected by

the resolution which took place in lhe.tr affairs when the sudden emancipation of the Negroes was effe.cled in July last, and what injluence may a be consideted that this occurrence will hare, as well on the value of private property generally, as on the value of those not quite trifling þÿ Asserts, belonging to the State Treasury in the West Indies f" 1 have been induced to make tins interpellation, partly because 1 have been tequesled to do so hy esteemed fellow-citizens, and also because it appears to me, that the events which have occurred in the lar distant Islands belonging to Denmark and the serious occurrences ot these latter times in the mother country, have, if not in the same degree, at least some claim to be discussed in tins house. It will be remembered by the honorable assembly, that a revolt broke out in the month of July last among the negro population of the Danish W. 1. Islands, in consequence whereof the functionary entrusted with the supreme power, the Governor General, by a proclamation of 3d July declared all unfree to tic liberated from that day. The question about emancipation was thus at once solved. It had already for a considerable time attracted the attention in this country of several estimable and pious men. who felt warmly for the value of man and ft is right of liberty, and of whom some are sealed in tins house ; but 1 think, that as much as they might have wished to accelerate the solution of this question, still they would have desired it to come in the

manner it did. However, 1 shall not now enter into a discussion of the diirerenl ! opinions which may exist for or against Negro Emancipation; nor shall 1 touch upon another question, which has been raised more that; once, when Colonial matters have been

discussed, I mean in how far it would lie advantageous for this country to dispose of net colonies þÿ that question cannot be decided as matters and circumstances have now turned. 1 shall pass by these questions ; my interpellation has principally beeo made in order to prove to liiose fellow citizens, which we have in a far distant part of the world, that those events, which have occurred withþÿInterpellation, in their limits, has not been unnoticed here ; and it appeals to me. that they have a claim , to this, as they have not on their part, neglected to show sympathy for the holy and just war in which the mother country has been involved, and have sent us considerable contributions in money I have also purported to draw the atiention of this house to the importance with regard to financial matters of a decided and regulating interference in the internal concerns of our colonies 1 shall observe, that the interest and prosperity of the inhabitants of the colonies depends materially upon the production of the islands and that all work has hitherto been done, and could only be done by slaves, and it was in consequence necessary foi the inhabitants to acquire slaves as property. These circumstances have existed for a long seiies of years and thev have been confirmed by ottr gov. eminent by uiflerent laws, some of them of a very late date. In a Placard of 1833 negro slaves were denominated by the Government as sacred property, and although it must be said for the honour ol our Government, that

it has always been most attentive to alleviate the condition of the negroes and secure them as far as possible against arbitrary and improper treatment ; yet, the right of property and disposal ot the slaves, belonging to the proprietors, were always acknowledged þÿ This was done in 1834. by a Placard, in w hich it was stated, that the liberty of negro slaves could only be granted on their finding the means of indemnifying their owners þÿ The same was repealed in 1840, and the argument then used was, that the regulations made in 1834 had proved suitable and proper, and the full disposal of the slaves, appei taining to the owner, was again acknowledged. The last mentioned law was accompanied by a circular from the Gove: nor- General, in which he expressly stated, that he tegarded the right, which tbo proprietor has to the labour of the nnfree, as guaranteed hy law, as indisputable and that tie could not he deprived thereof without compensation þÿ However melancholy it is to contemplate these matters, and however revolting it is to our better feelings, that a being, called our follow, should have been made the object of purchase .and sale, still it cannot be denied, that a right of prnpeity has existed in this respect, and that it has been guaranteed tiy the laws of the State. It appears to me, that when this is to he altered, which I consider necessary end verv desitahle for the interest of humanity ; the State cannot entirely throw iisido its dfttv to regard this matter, and that

the Government ought in this instance, as in in others, where the individual property is disposed vl lor state purposes, to he prepared to allow the patties interested a suitable indemnification. It may perhaps he said against this, that now the step has been taken, and without the fault ol Government ; hut I am free to answer, that it may still he questionable, whether the Government may be pronounced free from all responsibility in thisrespect, and more particularly, i! the meas-

ures taken in the colonies were of a nature to secure the public peace and order, and that protection of property, to which the citizens have a claim, l should think, as well there as elsewhere. It lias for instance been stated that the colonies were deprived of the means k> keep the sovereignty of the laws inviolate ; and it is to be observed that those whose duty it was to watch over the security of the country and its inhabitants, did not immediately take the necessary steps, at least not the most energetic steps to quell the insurrection. Hut i shall not in this respect enter upon a further consideration of t he question, more particularly because it would refer to persons and measures, which are now no doubt the subject of investigation, and no opinion could be weil founded, before these investigations have been closed. I shall call the attention of the house to a fact, that wherever emancipation has been carried out, it has been considered necessary, that the Slate should acknowledge, that those who suffered by it, should be compensated The example ot England no doubt known to most members heie, and I shall add, that when France had in April last decreed the emancipation o! their slaves, it was immediately after proposed to grant ninety millions of francs to indemnity the parties interested. þÿ It will aiso be remembered by most of the honorable members, that the question about the emancipation of the negroes has before this been discussed by the State Assemblies; their deliberations did not lead them to ihe

result to pronounce a decided opinion with regard to the question about indemnification, they asked for a committee to make those local examinations, which were necessary to propose the emancipation, but as I observed, they did not investigate the question of indemnification. and nothing has in this respect, been decided either way, for or against. Ttie same was the case with the Rescripts and Regulations aftei wards sent to the West India Government. No promise of compen Ration was given, a local investigation was ordered before emancipation could take place; bm. it ought to be well noticed, Government granted a term of 12 years, in the expiration of which, and not before, the negroes should be free. Whether litis term and tliu intermediate slate should lie a substitute for com peiisation, it is difficult to say. Now i fie emancipation has taken place, without the said teun having been used lor the benefit of the inhabitants, during which there should, no doubt have been taken measures to alleviate the losses of the owners, for instance by proper schools for the youth and by certain regulations for that degree ul lihettv, which would have been conceded the negroes ; and as ttie term i meiitiouo 1 tias become impossible by that sudden and unexpected event, it appears to me, that it ought to tie considered bv the Government, if no other means could be thought of, by which the inhabitants of the colonies might be assisted and the welfare of the colonies generally in a meas-

ure secured, I shall not lake upon myself to say in what manner ibis might lie done, whether by a loan, by facilitating and taking of taxes and other burthens, or bv a direct payment to tin greatest sufferers; but above all I think Government ought to consider, 1 tint a state of security is necessary and must lie obtained lor the inhabitants These observations 1 had to make with regard to the situation and condition ol the Colonists and

3 T. C 'JB 0 2 X Jl'TiS. their prosperity . Rut mV question had also ttie object of dinwiug the attention of this house to the importance for the slate itself, of preserving property and preventing the deterioration thereof in the colonies With regard to the Assetis of the State Treasury, 1 shall say, that from the last published Financial Accounts lor 140, the state holds Ileal Property in the West Indies to the value of 1,702,485 Rank dollars and Loans and Mortgages for 2,203,1 43 Rank dollars, total 3,005,028, or about four millions Rank dollars. It is evident, that unless care is taken to provide means for continuing the production and cultivation of the colonies, and having the necessary amount of labour disposable, the value of all ibis property will materially decrease.
